title: Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel
summary: David Ben-Gurion read the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel at the Tel Aviv Museum hours before the British Mandate ended. The United States extended de facto recognition that night and the Soviet Union recognised the state three days later. For Palestinian Arabs the period is remembered as the Nakba; fighting that had begun after the UN partition vote of November 1947 now became an interstate war.

title: Palestinian displacement of 1947-1949 (the Nakba)
summary: Between late 1947 and 1949 most Palestinian Arabs in the territory that became Israel fled or were expelled. Estimates range from about 520,000-600,000 (Israeli government figures) through c. 700,000 (Morris) and 711,000 (UN Conciliation Commission) to over 900,000 (some Palestinian researchers). Between 369 (Morris) and 418 (Khalidi) Arab villages were depopulated, most later destroyed or resettled; Israel barred return, and the refugees and their descendants became UNRWA's caseload.

displacement.note: Israeli government est. 520-600k (per Karsh); Morris c. 700k; UNCCP 711k (1950); Abu-Sitta 935k; UNRWA registered 957k in 1950

title: Arab states' armies enter the former Mandate territory
summary: The day after the declaration, forces of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the former Mandate territory; Transjordan's Arab Legion operated mainly in areas allotted to the Arab state and in the Jerusalem zone. Over the whole 1947-49 war, Israel's official count is 6,373 dead (about 4,000 soldiers and 2,400 civilians); historians estimate 3,700-7,000 dead among the Arab armies and 3,000-13,000 Palestinian Arab dead, fighters and civilians.

title: Israel Defense Forces established
summary: Ben-Gurion signed the Israel Defense Forces Ordinance, creating a single national army from the Haganah and banning other armed forces; members of the Irgun and Lehi were absorbed in the following weeks.

title: First truce of the 1948 war
summary: A UN-brokered four-week truce took effect on 11 June 1948 under mediator Folke Bernadotte. Both sides used it to reorganise and acquire arms despite an embargo; fighting resumed on 8 July.

title: The Altalena affair
summary: The Irgun ship Altalena arrived during the truce carrying about 940 volunteers and a large arms cargo. Ben-Gurion had accepted Begin's request that 20% of the arms go to the Jerusalem Battalion, but the two sides deadlocked over the rest; the government ordered the IDF to take the ship, and it was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on 22 June. Sixteen Irgun fighters and three IDF soldiers were killed (some accounts give a higher total); Begin ordered his men not to retaliate, and the Irgun was disbanded into the IDF.

choices.label: Order the IDF to seize the ship and its arms by force
choices.note: Ben-Gurion's government ordered the ship taken; it was shelled off Tel Aviv on 22 June 1948.

choices.label: Accept the Irgun's demand that the remaining arms go first to Irgun battalions
choices.note: Begin's position in the negotiations: after the agreed 20% for Jerusalem, arms to be distributed to Irgun units inside the IDF.

choices.label: Allow only the agreed 20% for the Jerusalem Battalion and keep negotiating over the rest
choices.note: The point both sides had already agreed before talks broke down.

title: Operation Dani and the expulsion from Lydda and Ramle
summary: In the 'Ten Days' between the truces, Operation Dani captured Lydda, Ramle and the airfield. On 12-13 July the remaining inhabitants were expelled toward Arab Legion lines: Morris gives 50,000-60,000 people, the Institute for Palestine Studies about 70,000 including neighbouring villages; many died of thirst and exhaustion on the march. Palestinian sources put those killed in Lydda at more than 400, including at the Dahmash mosque.

displacement.note: Morris (1986): 50-60,000 remaining inhabitants expelled; IPS/PalQuest: c. 70,000 incl. neighbouring villages

title: Second truce
summary: A second UN truce took effect on 18 July 1948 and lasted, with breaches, until Israel's October offensives in the Negev and Galilee.

title: Assassination of UN mediator Folke Bernadotte
summary: Count Folke Bernadotte, the UN mediator, and French observer Colonel André Sérot were shot dead in Jerusalem by members of Lehi, who opposed his proposals to modify the partition borders and internationalise Jerusalem. The killing drew international condemnation; the government outlawed Lehi.

title: Operation Yoav and the capture of Beersheba
summary: Israel broke the Egyptian lines in the northern Negev in Operation Yoav (also called the Ten Plagues). Beersheba was taken on 21 October 1948; its Arab inhabitants had left and the town was empty. Egyptian forces at Faluja were encircled.

title: Operation Hiram in the Upper Galilee
summary: Four IDF brigades took the Upper Galilee from the Arab Liberation Army in three days and pushed into southern Lebanon. Morris documents killings of civilians and prisoners at Safsaf, Jish and other villages and the flight or expulsion of many villagers north to Lebanon.

title: UN General Assembly Resolution 194
summary: The General Assembly resolved that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date, with compensation for those choosing not to return, and created the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine. Israel's position was that return could only be addressed in a peace settlement; the resolution remains central to Palestinian claims.

title: Operation Horev
summary: The IDF drove Egyptian forces out of most of the Negev and crossed into Sinai toward El Arish. Britain threatened to intervene under its treaty with Egypt, and Israel withdrew from Sinai; the operation ended on 7 January 1949 and Egypt agreed to armistice talks.

title: First Knesset election
summary: Israel's first general election, for a Constituent Assembly that renamed itself the Knesset, gave Ben-Gurion's Mapai 46 of 120 seats; turnout was 87%. Chaim Weizmann was chosen as the first President and Ben-Gurion formed a coalition government.

title: Israel-Egypt General Armistice Agreement
summary: Signed at Rhodes under UN mediator Ralph Bunche. Egypt kept the Gaza Strip, now crowded with refugees; the encircled Egyptian brigade at Faluja was evacuated.

title: Operation Uvda reaches Umm Rashrash (Eilat)
summary: The last operation of the war secured the southern Negev; IDF units reached the Gulf of Aqaba at Umm Rashrash on 10 March 1949 (some sources give 13 March) and raised the improvised 'Ink Flag'. In December 1949 a group from the Kibbutz ha-Me'uhad movement set up a temporary camp there, the nucleus of Eilat.

title: Israel-Lebanon General Armistice Agreement
summary: Signed at Ras en Naqura (Rosh Hanikra); the armistice line followed the Mandate-era international border and Israel withdrew from villages it had taken in southern Lebanon during Operation Hiram.

title: Austerity (tzena) and rationing
summary: Facing mass immigration and a foreign-currency crisis, the government under Dov Yosef, Minister of Rationing and Supply, introduced rationing of food, clothing and furniture. The austerity regime lasted, in diminishing form, through the 1950s, and a black market flourished.

title: Israel-Jordan General Armistice Agreement
summary: Signed at Rhodes. Jerusalem was divided, with Jordan holding the Old City and East Jerusalem, and the West Bank remained under Jordanian control; the 'Little Triangle' of Arab villages (including Umm al-Fahm, Tayibe and Kafr Qasim) passed to Israel and its residents became Israeli citizens.

title: Israel admitted to the United Nations
summary: General Assembly Resolution 273 admitted Israel as the 59th member by 37 votes to 12 with 9 abstentions, following Security Council Resolution 69. Arab states voted against.

title: Operation Magic Carpet (On Wings of Eagles)
summary: Some 49,000 Jews, nearly all from Yemen (Alaska Airlines records 48,818), were flown to Israel from a JDC transit camp in Aden in about 380 flights between June 1949 and September 1950. Many arrivals were placed in immigrant camps.

title: Immigrant camp at Khalisa becomes Kiryat Shmona
summary: Yemenite immigrants settled at the depopulated Arab village of al-Khalisa in the Hula Valley in July 1949; the camp became the town of Kiryat Shmona, named for Joseph Trumpeldor and seven others killed at Tel Hai in 1920. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates its foundation as a permanent town to 1950; it received local-council status in 1953.

title: Israel-Syria General Armistice Agreement
summary: Signed at Hill 232 near Mahanayim, the last of the four armistices. Syria withdrew from areas it held west of the international border, which became demilitarized zones; disputes over the DMZs and water fed clashes for the next 18 years. Iraq signed no armistice; its forces withdrew and Jordan took over their sector.

title: UNRWA created for Palestine refugees
summary: General Assembly Resolution 302 (IV) established the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East; it began operations on 1 May 1950, serving about 750,000 refugees in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.

title: Knesset proclaims Jerusalem the capital
summary: After the UN General Assembly reaffirmed internationalisation of Jerusalem on 9 December 1949, Ben-Gurion told the Knesset on 13 December that government institutions would move there; on 23 January 1950 the Knesset declared Jerusalem the capital. Most states did not recognise this and kept embassies in Tel Aviv; East Jerusalem remained under Jordan.

title: Absentees' Property Law
summary: The law vested the property of Palestinian Arabs who had left for Arab states or Arab-held parts of Palestine after 29 November 1947 in a Custodian of Absentees' Property, who transferred most land to a Development Authority and on to state and Jewish settlement use. It also applied to many Arab citizens who had been displaced within Israel ('present absentees'). Palestinian and human-rights groups regard it as the legal basis of large-scale dispossession.

title: Jordan annexes the West Bank
summary: A joint session of Jordan's parliament approved the annexation of the West Bank and East Jerusalem, whose residents had been given Jordanian citizenship. Only Britain and Pakistan are generally recorded as recognising the annexation; the Arab League treated Jordan as trustee.

title: Ma'abarot transit camps
summary: To house the flood of new immigrants, the state and Jewish Agency set up ma'abarot - tent and tin-shack camps near towns and farms. By the end of 1951 roughly 220,000-250,000 people, a majority from Middle Eastern and North African countries, lived in about 125 of them; many became development towns and the last closed around 1963.

title: Law of Return
summary: The Knesset enacted the Law of Return, giving every Jew the right to immigrate to Israel as an oleh. It became the legal foundation for later aliyah waves; Palestinian refugees had no equivalent right of return.

title: Remaining Arab residents of Majdal transferred to Gaza
summary: Al-Majdal was taken by Israel on 5 November 1948; about 2,700 Arab inhabitants remained, of whom some 500 were deported in December 1948. In 1950 most of the rest were moved to the Egyptian-held Gaza Strip; the move was officially presented as voluntary, while historians including Morris describe pressure and coercion. The town was resettled by Jewish immigrants and became Ashkelon.

displacement.note: c. 2,700 remained after Nov 1948; c. 500 deported Dec 1948, most of the rest moved in 1950 (Morris; O. Cohen)

title: Har-Tuv transit camp, nucleus of Beit Shemesh
summary: A ma'abara for Bulgarian Jewish immigrants was set up at Har-Tuv in the Jerusalem corridor; joined by immigrants from Iran, Iraq, Romania, Morocco and Kurdistan, its residents began moving into permanent housing at Beit Shemesh in 1952.

title: Operation Ezra and Nehemiah: airlift of Iraqi Jews
summary: After Iraq allowed Jews to emigrate on condition of giving up citizenship and liquidating property, more than 120,000 (by some counts about 130,000) Iraqi Jews were flown to Israel, mostly in 1951 and early 1952, leaving about 6,000 in Iraq. Emigrants could take $140 and 30 kg of luggage; most arrived destitute and were housed in ma'abarot.

title: Draining of Lake Hula
summary: KKL-JNF began draining Lake Hula and its swamps in 1951, completing the work in 1957-58 to create farmland and reduce malaria. The valley's Arab villages had been depopulated in 1948. The drainage later caused environmental damage, including sinking soils and harm to Sea of Galilee water quality, leading to partial re-flooding in the 1990s.

title: Yeruham founded
summary: Kfar Yeruham was founded in the central Negev as one of the first development towns, near the Large Makhtesh, an area then thought rich in minerals.

title: Sderot and Mitzpe Ramon founded
summary: Sderot was established beside the Gevim-Dorot transit camp in the northwestern Negev, first housing Kurdish and Persian Jewish immigrants who lived in tents and shacks until 1954. Mitzpe Ramon began as a camp for workers building the road to Eilat.

title: Second Knesset election
summary: Mapai won 45 seats and the General Zionists rose to 20; turnout was 75.1%. Ben-Gurion formed a new coalition.

title: Mass immigration doubles the population
summary: Israel's population grew from 806,000 in 1948 to 1,578,000 at the end of 1951, mostly through immigration of Holocaust survivors from Europe and of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, over 260,000 of whom had arrived by 1951 as communities in Iraq, Yemen, Libya and elsewhere left amid hostility and legal pressure. Absorption strained housing, food supplies and the budget.

title: Knesset debate on German reparations
summary: After West Germany offered to negotiate compensation, the Knesset debated direct talks for three days. Menachem Begin led a mass rally against 'blood money' that turned violent outside the Knesset; on 9 January the Knesset approved negotiations by 61 to 50.

choices.label: Authorise direct negotiations with West Germany
choices.note: Ben-Gurion's government; approved 61-50 on 9 January 1952.

choices.label: Refuse any direct dealings with Germany
choices.note: Position of Herut under Begin and of others in the opposition who called the payments 'blood money'.

choices.label: Pursue claims only through the four Allied powers
choices.note: Israel's initial route: Sharett's note of 12 March 1951 claimed $1.5 billion via the US, UK, France and USSR.

title: Reparations Agreement signed in Luxembourg
summary: Moshe Sharett and Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed an agreement under which West Germany would pay Israel 3 billion marks, largely in goods and services over 12-14 years, plus 450 million marks to the Claims Conference. It entered into force in March 1953 and financed ships, rail, power and industrial equipment.

title: President Chaim Weizmann dies
summary: Israel's first president, the chemist and Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann, died in office; the Knesset elected Yitzhak Ben-Zvi to succeed him.

title: Qibya raid
summary: After infiltrators from the West Bank killed a mother and her two children at Yehud, IDF Unit 101 under Ariel Sharon raided the Jordanian-held village of Qibya, blowing up some 45-50 houses and killing 69 villagers, many hiding inside. The raid was condemned internationally, including by UN Security Council Resolution 101.

title: Ben-Gurion retires to Sde Boker; Sharett becomes Prime Minister
summary: David Ben-Gurion left the government at the end of 1953 and joined Kibbutz Sde Boker in the Negev as a symbol of settling the desert. Foreign Minister Moshe Sharett became Prime Minister in January 1954.

title: Kiryat Gat founded
summary: Kiryat Gat began in 1954 as a ma'abara near the depopulated village of Iraq al-Manshiyya and was established as the centre of the Lachish development region in 1955, initially by families from Morocco.

title: Operation Susannah and the Lavon affair
summary: An Israeli military-intelligence cell of Egyptian Jews planted incendiary devices at post offices, US information libraries and a British-owned cinema in Alexandria and Cairo, aiming to keep British troops in the Canal Zone. The network was caught; two members were hanged in early 1955 and others died in custody or were imprisoned. Defence Minister Pinhas Lavon resigned in February 1955; whether he gave the order became a political scandal that resurfaced in 1960-61.

title: Bank of Israel established
summary: The Bank of Israel opened as the central bank, taking over currency issue; David Horowitz served as its first governor until 1971.

title: Gaza raid (Operation Black Arrow)
summary: Israeli paratroopers attacked an Egyptian army base near Gaza City in reprisal for fedayeen infiltrations, killing 37-38 Egyptian soldiers for 8 Israeli dead. Historians including Shlaim link the raid to Egypt's decision later that year to buy Soviet-bloc arms through Czechoslovakia and to sponsor fedayeen raids.

title: Kasztner libel verdict
summary: In a libel case brought by the state on behalf of government official Rudolf Kasztner, Judge Benjamin Halevi found that Kasztner, a leader of Hungarian Jewry in 1944, had 'sold his soul to the devil' in negotiating with Eichmann. The ruling shook Mapai before the election. Kasztner was shot in Tel Aviv in March 1957 and died days later; in January 1958 the Supreme Court largely overturned the verdict.

title: Third Knesset election; Ben-Gurion returns
summary: Mapai fell to 40 seats while Herut rose to 15; turnout was 82.8%. Ben-Gurion, back in the cabinet as Defence Minister after Lavon's resignation, again became Prime Minister in November 1955, with Sharett remaining Foreign Minister until June 1956.

title: Dimona and Ofakim founded
summary: The first residents moved to Dimona on 1 August 1955, a new town for workers of the Dead Sea Works and nearby phosphate fields; Ofakim was founded the same year as the centre of the Merhavim development region. Both were settled mainly by immigrants from North Africa.

title: Ashdod and Netivot founded
summary: Modern Ashdod was founded at the mouth of Nahal Lachish near the site of the Arab town of Isdud, whose inhabitants had left with retreating Egyptian forces in 1948; its deep-water port opened in 1965. Netivot was founded the same year in the northwestern Negev, mainly by immigrants from Tunisia and Morocco.

title: Kafr Qasim massacre
summary: On the first evening of the Sinai war, Border Police enforcing a curfew brought forward without warning shot dead Arab citizens of Kafr Qasim returning from work; the toll is given as 47-49, including women and children (49 is most often cited). In 1958 a military court sentenced the convicted officers and policemen to 7-17 years and established that a 'manifestly unlawful order' must be refused.

title: Sinai Campaign (Suez War)
summary: Under the secret Sèvres protocol with Britain and France, Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October 1956; Britain and France issued an ultimatum and attacked the Canal Zone. Israel took Gaza and all of Sinai to Sharm el-Sheikh within days; a ceasefire took effect on 7-8 November under UN General Assembly resolutions. Israeli dead are given as 172 (AP) to 189 (EBSCO); Egyptian dead are estimated at roughly 1,000 to 3,000.

choices.label: Join the Anglo-French plan agreed at Sèvres
choices.note: Ben-Gurion, Dayan and Peres agreed the Sèvres protocol of 22-24 October 1956 (Shlaim).

choices.label: Continue limited reprisal raids against fedayeen bases without a full war
choices.note: The pre-war reprisal policy of 1953-56 (Qibya, Gaza raid) as described by Shlaim.

choices.label: Seek arms and a security guarantee from France without going to war
choices.note: France was already supplying arms in 1956; restraint was the line associated with Sharett, who left office in June 1956 (Shlaim).

title: Nazareth Illit (Nof HaGalil) founded
summary: A Jewish town was built by the state on the hills above Arab Nazareth, with first dwellings completed in September 1956; it took the name Nazareth Illit in 1958 and was renamed Nof HaGalil in 2019. Historian Geremy Forman describes its purpose as consolidating state control over the Arab city.

title: Withdrawal from Sinai and Gaza; UNEF deployed
summary: Under US pressure and General Assembly resolutions 1124 and 1125, Israel announced on 1 March 1957 that it would withdraw. UNEF entered Gaza on 6-8 March and took over Sharm el-Sheikh by 12 March, guaranteeing passage through the Straits of Tiran to Eilat until 1967.

choices.label: Withdraw fully in exchange for UNEF at Sharm el-Sheikh and freedom of navigation
choices.note: Announced 1-4 March 1957 after GA resolutions 1124/1125.

choices.label: Keep holding the Gaza Strip and Sharm el-Sheikh in defiance of the General Assembly
choices.note: Israel's position from January to February 1957, when it withdrew from the rest of Sinai but retained these two areas (UN record).

title: Franco-Israeli agreement on the Dimona reactor
summary: France agreed to build a 24-megawatt research reactor near Dimona, constructed in secret outside IAEA inspection. Ben-Gurion acknowledged the reactor publicly in December 1960, describing it as for peaceful purposes, and gave the US assurances to that effect; it went critical in 1964. Israel maintains a policy of nuclear ambiguity.

title: Wadi Salib riots in Haifa
summary: Police shot and wounded Moroccan-born Akiva Elkrif in Wadi Salib, a former Arab quarter of Haifa housing North African immigrants in poor conditions. Protests led by the Union of North African Immigrants spread to other towns and brought discrimination against Mizrahi Jews into national politics.

title: Fourth Knesset election
summary: Mapai won its best result, 47 seats; Herut took 17. Turnout was 81.6%.

title: Mossad captures Adolf Eichmann
summary: Mossad agents seized Adolf Eichmann, a principal organiser of the Holocaust, near his home in Buenos Aires and flew him secretly to Israel; Ben-Gurion announced the capture to the Knesset on 23 May 1960. Argentina protested the violation of its sovereignty at the UN Security Council.

title: Arad founded
summary: The planned desert town of Arad was founded in the eastern Negev in an area formerly used by Bedouin tribes.

title: Eichmann trial
summary: The trial opened in Jerusalem before a special panel headed by Judge Moshe Landau, with Attorney-General Gideon Hausner prosecuting; testimony from survivors made the Holocaust central to Israeli and world awareness. Eichmann was sentenced to death on 15 December 1961 and hanged at Ramla on the night of 31 May-1 June 1962, the only civil execution in Israel's history.

title: Shavit 2 sounding rocket launched
summary: Israel launched its first rocket, the two-stage Shavit 2, from the Mediterranean coast. Its meteorological aims were not met, but it was publicised as a technological milestone.

title: Fifth Knesset election
summary: Held early after the Lavon affair re-erupted, the election cut Mapai to 42 seats; turnout was 81.6%. Ben-Gurion formed his last government.

title: Operation Yachin: emigration of Moroccan Jews
summary: After emigration from Morocco had been banned since 1959 and the clandestine boat Egoz sank with 44 aboard in January 1961, a Mossad-run arrangement with the Moroccan government, financed via HIAS payments, allowed about 97,000 Jews to leave by spring 1964 (estimates range from 80,000 to 100,000); most went to Israel, some to France, Canada or the US.

title: Levi Eshkol becomes Prime Minister
summary: David Ben-Gurion resigned on 16 June 1963, citing personal reasons, and Finance Minister Levi Eshkol, a founder of the Mekorot water company, formed a government later that month. In 1965 Ben-Gurion split from Mapai to found Rafi.

title: Karmiel founded
summary: Karmiel was established in the Beit HaKerem Valley as a planned development town, part of a policy to increase the Jewish population of the Galilee.

title: Palestine Liberation Organization founded
summary: At the Arab League's initiative, a Palestinian congress in Jordanian-held East Jerusalem proclaimed the PLO and adopted a National Charter, with Ahmad Shuqeiri as chairman.

title: National Water Carrier begins operating
summary: The National Water Carrier, built by Mekorot, began pumping water from the Sea of Galilee to the centre and the northern Negev. Arab states saw it as diverting Jordan basin water; the Arab League launched a headwaters diversion plan, and Israeli-Syrian clashes over the works followed in 1964-67.

title: Diplomatic relations with West Germany
title_he: כינון יחסים דיפלומטיים עם גרמניה המערבית
summary: Israel and the Federal Republic of Germany exchanged notes establishing diplomatic relations; ambassadors took up their posts in August 1965 amid protests in Israel. Most Arab League states broke relations with Bonn in response.

title: Sixth Knesset election
summary: The Mapai-led Alignment won 45 seats, the new Gahal bloc of Herut and the Liberals 26, and Ben-Gurion's breakaway Rafi 10; turnout was 83.0%. Eshkol remained Prime Minister.

title: Samu raid
summary: In response to Fatah attacks launched from the West Bank, the IDF mounted a large daytime raid on the Jordanian-held village of as-Samu, demolishing dozens of houses and fighting Jordanian troops. Jordanian casualties were reported as 16 killed and 54 wounded, and one Israeli soldier was killed. The Security Council censured Israel in Resolution 228, and unrest in the West Bank against King Hussein followed.

title: Military government over Arab citizens abolished
summary: The military government imposed in 1948 on Arab-populated areas of Israel under British-era emergency regulations, which restricted movement and required permits, was abolished effective 1 December 1966. Permit powers passed to the police and some restrictions continued under emergency regulations.

choices.label: Abolish military government from 1 December 1966
choices.note: Eshkol's decision, announced to the Knesset in November 1966.

choices.label: Keep the military government in place
choices.note: Policy until 1966; abolition bills in 1963 were defeated (JTA/ECF).

title: S. Y. Agnon awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature
title_he: ש"י עגנון זוכה בפרס נובל לספרות
summary: Shmuel Yosef Agnon shared the 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature with the German-Jewish poet Nelly Sachs, the first Nobel prize for an Israeli and for Hebrew literature.

title: Straits of Tiran closed: the 'waiting period'
summary: Egypt moved troops into Sinai from 15 May 1967, Nasser ordered the UN Emergency Force out on 18 May, and on 23 May Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. During the following 'waiting period' Foreign Minister Abba Eban sought Western diplomatic support, including a proposed international flotilla, while reservists were mobilised. A national unity government was formed on 1 June with Moshe Dayan as defence minister, and on 4 June the cabinet authorised military action.

choices.label: Exhaust diplomacy briefly, then strike first (cabinet decision of 4 June)
choices.note: The cabinet authorised the defence establishment to decide timing on 4 June; the air strike followed on 5 June (S200).

choices.label: Keep waiting for a US-British international flotilla to reopen the straits
choices.note: The 'Regatta' flotilla proposal and Eban's mission were the diplomatic track pursued in late May (S289).

title: Displacement of Palestinians and Syrians in 1967
summary: During and after the war a large part of the population of the newly occupied areas left or was expelled. By December 1967 about 245,000 people had crossed from the West Bank and Gaza Strip to Jordan and about 11,000 from Gaza to Egypt; other historians estimate 280,000-325,000 Palestinians displaced overall. From the Golan Heights, estimates of Syrians who fled or were expelled range from about 80,000 (Morris) to about 116,000 including Palestinians (McDowall). Few were allowed to return.

displacement.note: McDowall (1989): ~245,000 to Jordan and 11,000 to Egypt by Dec 1967; Bowker (2003): 280,000-325,000.
Morris: ~80,000 Syrians; McDowall: ~116,000 Palestinians and Syrians combined.

title: Six-Day War
summary: Israel launched pre-emptive air strikes on Egypt on 5 June 1967; Jordan and Syria entered the fighting, and by the ceasefire of 10 June Israel held the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. Israeli deaths are given as 776-983. Arab fatality estimates vary widely: roughly 9,800-15,000 Egyptian, about 700-800 Jordanian and 1,000-2,500 Syrian dead. Israel now governed more than three-quarters of a million Palestinians in the occupied territories.

title: East Jerusalem placed under Israeli law and municipality
title_he: איחוד ירושלים והחלת המשפט הישראלי במזרח העיר
summary: On 27-28 June 1967 Israel extended the Jerusalem municipal boundary to take in East Jerusalem and about 70 km2 of surrounding West Bank land and applied Israeli law and administration there. The UN General Assembly, in resolution 2253 of 4 July 1967, considered the measures invalid and called on Israel to rescind them.

title: The Allon Plan
summary: Deputy Prime Minister Yigal Allon proposed that Israel keep the Jordan Valley, East Jerusalem and the Etzion bloc while returning the densely populated West Bank hill areas to Jordan or to Palestinian self-rule. An initial version based on Palestinian autonomy was rejected by most ministers on 30 July 1967. The plan was never formally adopted, but in 1968 most ministers treated it as the basis of settlement policy. (On 19 June the cabinet had secretly decided to offer Sinai and the Golan for peace with Egypt and Syria.)

choices.label: Leave the plan formally unadopted but use it as an informal guide (Jordan Valley, Etzion bloc settlement)
choices.note: Never officially endorsed; backed by most ministers as a policy basis in 1968 (S225).

choices.label: Adopt Allon's original version: Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank hill areas
choices.note: Allon's first version, rejected by most ministers on 30 July 1967 (S225).

choices.label: Seek a 'Jordanian option': return populated areas to King Hussein in a peace deal
choices.note: Allon shifted to the 'Jordanian option' in early 1968 (S225).

title: Kfar Etzion re-established
summary: In September 1967 a group led by Hanan Porat, including children of the kibbutz's 1948 defenders, re-established Kfar Etzion in the West Bank with cabinet approval, despite legal advice that civilian settlement in occupied territory would contravene the Fourth Geneva Convention. It is generally regarded as the first Israeli settlement in the West Bank after 1967.

title: Khartoum Resolution: 'three no's'
summary: An Arab League summit in Khartoum resolved on 1 September 1967 on 'no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it', while pledging to work to remove the effects of the June war.

title: Destroyer INS Eilat sunk
summary: Egyptian Komar-class missile boats fired Soviet-made Styx missiles at the Israeli destroyer Eilat off Port Said on 21 October 1967, sinking it; 47 of its 199 crew were killed or missing. Israel retaliated by shelling the oil refineries at Port Suez.

title: UN Security Council Resolution 242
summary: The Security Council unanimously adopted resolution 242, emphasising the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war and calling for 'withdrawal of Israel armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' together with an end to belligerency and recognition of every state's right to live within secure and recognised boundaries, freedom of navigation and a just settlement of the refugee problem. Arab states read it as requiring withdrawal from all territories; Israel read it as linked to negotiated borders.

title: Submarine INS Dakar lost
summary: The newly acquired submarine Dakar disappeared in the eastern Mediterranean on its delivery voyage from Britain after its last signal on 25 January 1968, with all 69 crew. The wreck was located between Crete and Cyprus in May 1999.

title: Battle of Karameh
summary: Israeli forces raided the Fatah base at Karameh in the Jordan Valley in response to guerrilla attacks; Jordanian army units joined the fighting. Israeli dead are given as 28-33, Jordanian as about 40-84 and Palestinian fighters as about 100-200. Israel withdrew the same day; Fatah presented the battle as a victory and recruitment to Palestinian guerrilla groups rose sharply.

title: Settlers in Hebron; Kiryat Arba established
summary: In April 1968 a group led by Rabbi Moshe Levinger held a Passover seder at the Park Hotel in Hebron and refused to leave. The government later moved them to a military compound and in 1970-71 built Kiryat Arba on the city's edge, on land requisitioned 'for military purposes', according to minutes of a July 1970 meeting in Defence Minister Dayan's office. It became a local council in 1979.

title: Tel Aviv hosts the Summer Paralympics
summary: Israel hosted the third Summer Paralympic Games from 4 to 13 November 1968, with the opening in Jerusalem and events in Ramat Gan; about 750 athletes from 28-29 nations took part, and Israel won 62 medals.

title: Commando raid on Beirut airport
title_he: פשיטת הקומנדו על נמל התעופה בביירות (מבצע תשורה)
summary: After a PFLP attack on an El Al airliner in Athens, Israeli commandos raided Beirut International Airport on 28 December 1968 and destroyed 13-14 Lebanese civilian aircraft; no casualties were reported. The Security Council condemned the raid in resolution 262 and France imposed an arms embargo on Israel.

title: Soviet Jewish immigration wave of the 1970s
title_he: גל העלייה מברית המועצות בשנות ה-70
summary: After years of restriction, emigration of Soviet Jews grew from 1969; about 163,000 Soviet Jews settled in Israel in the late 1960s and 1970s, most of them in 1969-1973. From the mid-1970s a growing share of emigrants chose the United States instead (47% in 1976). Total immigration to Israel from all countries peaked at 55,888 in 1972.

title: War of Attrition
summary: Artillery duels and raids along the Suez Canal, under way since 1967, escalated after Nasser declared a war of attrition in March 1969; Israel answered with commando raids and deep air strikes, and Soviet air-defence personnel deployed in Egypt. A US-brokered ceasefire took effect on 7-8 August 1970. Israeli military deaths are given as about 694-1,424 depending on period counted; Egyptian deaths are estimated at 2,882-10,000.

title: Golda Meir becomes Prime Minister
summary: Prime Minister Levi Eshkol died suddenly on 26 February 1969. Golda Meir formed the Fourteenth Government on 17 March 1969, continuing the national unity coalition.

title: Election to the Seventh Knesset
summary: The Alignment led by Golda Meir won 56 of 120 seats, the most any list had won, with Gahal at 26 and the National Religious Party at 12. The national unity coalition continued.

title: Ceasefire ends the War of Attrition
summary: A US-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Egypt took effect on the night of 7-8 August 1970, ending the War of Attrition along the Suez Canal.

title: Black September: Jordan expels the PLO
summary: After the PFLP's Dawson's Field hijackings (6-12 September 1970), the Jordanian army moved against Palestinian guerrilla organisations; a Syrian armoured incursion was turned back and Israel readied forces as Jordan asked Western governments for help. Estimates of Palestinian dead range from about 2,000 to 3,400 (Arafat claimed far more); the Jordanian army lost 537 killed. Fighting ended in July 1971 and the PLO relocated to Lebanon.

title: Israeli Black Panthers protests
summary: Young Mizrahi Jews, mostly of Moroccan origin, from Jerusalem's Musrara neighbourhood formed the Black Panthers in early 1971 to protest poverty and discrimination. After meeting them in April, Prime Minister Meir called them 'not nice'; the 'Night of the Panthers' rally on 18 May 1971 drew 5,000-7,000 people and ended in clashes and more than 100 arrests. A public committee acknowledged ethnic and socio-economic gaps and welfare spending rose.

title: Lod Airport massacre
summary: Three members of the Japanese Red Army, acting for the PFLP, opened fire in the arrivals hall at Lod Airport on 30 May 1972, killing 26 people - 17 Puerto Rican Christian pilgrims, 8 Israelis including biophysicist Aharon Katzir, and a Canadian - and wounding about 80. Two attackers died; Kozo Okamoto was captured.

title: Munich Olympics massacre
summary: Eight Black September militants seized members of the Israeli Olympic team in Munich on 5 September 1972; two were killed in the village and nine more during a failed West German rescue at Fürstenfeldbruck - 11 Israeli athletes and coaches in all - along with a West German police officer. Five attackers were killed; the three survivors were freed in October after the hijacking of a Lufthansa airliner. Israel responded with air strikes on bases in Syria and Lebanon and a covert campaign against those it held responsible.

choices.label: Authorise a covert campaign ('Committee X') against those held responsible
choices.note: Meir and Dayan headed 'Committee X', which authorised the operations (S232, S233).

choices.label: Limit the response to conventional strikes on guerrilla bases in Syria and Lebanon
choices.note: Air strikes on bases were carried out on 8 September 1972 (S232).

title: Libyan Arab Airlines Flight 114 shot down
summary: A Libyan Boeing 727 that had strayed over Israeli-held Sinai in a sandstorm was shot down by Israeli F-4 fighters on 21 February 1973 after failing to respond to interception signals; 108 of the 113 people aboard were killed. Declassified cabinet minutes show ministers decided to deny responsibility and refuse an official inquiry; Israel later paid compensation to victims' families.

title: Operation Spring of Youth (Beirut raid)
summary: Israeli commandos landed in Beirut on the night of 9-10 April 1973 and killed three senior PLO figures - Muhammad Yusuf al-Najjar, Kamal Adwan and Kamal Nasser - and attacked other PLO targets. Two Israeli soldiers were killed; Lebanon's complaint to the UN reported Lebanese policemen and civilians among the dead.

title: Yom Kippur War
summary: Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated surprise attack on Yom Kippur, 6 October 1973, crossing the Suez Canal and advancing on the Golan. Israel stopped the Syrian advance, counter-attacked toward Damascus and crossed the canal; a US airlift resupplied Israel from mid-October. Fighting ended on 24-25 October after resolution 338. Israeli dead are given as about 2,520-2,800; Egyptian estimates range from about 5,000 to 15,000 and Syrian from 3,000 to 3,500.

choices.label: Mobilise reserves on a large scale but forgo a pre-emptive strike
choices.note: Meir approved Elazar's mobilisation request but refused a pre-emptive strike so Israel would not be blamed and could count on US help (S209).

choices.label: Order the pre-emptive air strike on Syria proposed by Chief of Staff Elazar
choices.note: Elazar's 6 October morning proposal (S209).

choices.label: Limit the call-up to the air force and two armoured divisions
choices.note: Defence Minister Dayan's narrower mobilisation position on 6 October (S209).

title: UN Security Council Resolution 338
summary: The Council called for a ceasefire within 12 hours in the positions then held, implementation of resolution 242 and negotiations between the parties. Israel accepted immediately; fighting continued and resolution 339 followed on 23 October.

title: Agranat Commission of Inquiry appointed
summary: A state commission chaired by Supreme Court President Shimon Agranat was set up on 21 November 1973 to investigate the lead-up to the war. Its interim report on 1 April 1974 recommended removing the head of Military Intelligence and other officers and found Chief of Staff David Elazar responsible, but declined to rule on the ministers. Prime Minister Meir's government resigned about ten days later.

title: Election to the Eighth Knesset
summary: Held on 31 December 1973 after being postponed by the war, the election gave the Alignment 51 seats and the newly formed Likud 39. Meir formed a new coalition, which proved short-lived.

title: Israel-Egypt disengagement agreement (Sinai I)
summary: Under US mediation, Israel and Egypt agreed in January 1974 to separate their forces: Israel withdrew from the west bank of the Suez Canal to lines in western Sinai, with a UN buffer zone between the armies.

title: Gush Emunim founded
summary: Students of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook founded Gush Emunim ('Bloc of the Faithful') in February 1974 to promote Jewish settlement throughout the West Bank, Gaza and Golan. It became the main organiser of settlement attempts in the following years.

title: Kiryat Shmona attack
summary: Three militants who crossed from Lebanon attacked an apartment building in Kiryat Shmona on 11 April 1974, killing 18 people, about half of them children; the attackers died when their explosives detonated. The attack was claimed by the PFLP-General Command.

title: Ma'alot school attack
summary: Three DFLP militants from Lebanon killed residents of Ma'alot and on 15 May 1974 took more than 100 people, mostly teenage students on a school trip from Safed, hostage in a school. During the storming of the building 22 students and several adults were killed; total Israeli deaths, including those killed before the siege, are usually given as 25-31.

title: Israel-Syria separation of forces agreement
summary: After months of artillery exchanges on the Golan, Israel and Syria signed a separation of forces agreement on 31 May 1974. Israel withdrew from the salient captured in 1973 and from a strip including the town of Quneitra, which returned to Syrian civil administration; the Security Council established the UN Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) the same day.

title: Yitzhak Rabin becomes Prime Minister
summary: After Golda Meir and Defence Minister Dayan resigned following the Agranat interim report, Yitzhak Rabin formed the Seventeenth Government on 3 June 1974.

title: Ma'ale Adumim settlement begun
summary: A Gush Emunim group set up on a ridge east of Jerusalem in 1975 and was at first evicted; the government then approved a settlement. Ma'ale Adumim became a local council in 1979 and a city in 1991.

title: Yamit founded in north-eastern Sinai
summary: Construction of Yamit, planned as the urban centre of Israeli settlement in the Rafah salient of north-eastern Sinai, began in 1975 and the first residents arrived that year. It became the largest of 14 Sinai settlements (about 600 houses by 1982).

title: Sinai Interim Agreement (Sinai II)
summary: Signed in Geneva on 4 September 1975, the agreement committed Israel and Egypt to resolve their conflict by peaceful means, provided for a further Israeli withdrawal in Sinai and a new UN buffer zone, and deepened US involvement as mediator.

title: UN General Assembly resolution 3379
summary: The General Assembly adopted resolution 3379 by 72 votes to 35 with 32 abstentions, determining that 'zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination'. Israel and its allies rejected it; the Assembly revoked it in December 1991 (resolution 46/86).

title: Sebastia compromise: settlers at Kadum
summary: Garin Elon Moreh, linked to Gush Emunim, made eight attempts to settle at the old Ottoman railway station at Sebastia near Nablus and was removed by the army seven times. In late 1975 the Rabin government agreed to let about 25 families stay in the nearby Kadum army camp, the origin of the settlement of Kedumim and a turning point for settlement in the northern West Bank.

choices.label: Accept a compromise: settlers move into the Kadum army camp
choices.note: The compromise placed about 25 families at Kadum (S239).

choices.label: Continue forcible removal of the settlers, as on seven previous attempts
choices.note: The army had evicted the group seven times (S239).

choices.label: Authorise a settlement at Sebastia itself, as the settlers demanded
choices.note: The settlers' stated aim (S239).

title: Land Day
summary: Arab citizens of Israel held a general strike and demonstrations on 30 March 1976 against a government plan, published on 11 March, to expropriate about 20,000 dunams in the Galilee between Sakhnin and Arraba, about 6,300 of them Arab-owned. Six Arab citizens were killed by security forces, about 100 were wounded and hundreds arrested. The date is commemorated annually by Palestinians in Israel and the occupied territories.

choices.label: Proceed with the expropriation plan and deploy police and army against the strike
choices.note: What happened on 30 March 1976 (S241).

choices.label: Suspend the expropriation and negotiate with Arab local leaders
choices.note: The demand of the Arab committee that called the strike (S241).

title: Entebbe hijacking and rescue (Operation Thunderbolt)
summary: Air France Flight 139 from Tel Aviv was hijacked on 27 June 1976 by Palestinian and German militants and flown to Entebbe, Uganda, where Israeli and Jewish passengers were held. On the night of 3-4 July Israeli commandos rescued 102 of 106 hostages; three hostages were killed in the raid and a fourth, Dora Bloch, was later murdered in Uganda. The unit commander Yonatan Netanyahu, all seven hijackers and about 45 Ugandan soldiers were killed.

choices.label: Order a long-range military rescue
choices.note: Cabinet approved the raid on 3 July 1976 (S242).

choices.label: Negotiate the release of prisoners in exchange for the hostages
choices.note: The cabinet was reportedly prepared to negotiate if no military option was feasible; Rabin initially leaned this way (S242).

title: Katzrin founded on the Golan Heights
summary: Katzrin was established in 1977 as the planned urban centre for Israeli settlement on the Golan Heights, following a government decision of November 1973.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv wins the European Champions Cup
title_he: מכבי תל אביב זוכה בגביע אירופה
summary: Maccabi Tel Aviv beat Mobilgirgi Varese 78-77 in Belgrade on 7 April 1977 to win its first European basketball championship.

title: 1977 election: the 'Mahapakh'
summary: In the election of 17 May 1977 Likud won 43 seats and the Alignment fell to 32, with the new Democratic Movement for Change (Dash) taking 15. It was the first transfer of power from the Labour movement; Menachem Begin formed a government on 20 June 1977.

title: Sadat visits Jerusalem
summary: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat arrived in Israel on 19 November 1977, the first visit by an Arab head of state, and addressed the Knesset on 20 November, calling for peace based on Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian rights. Prime Minister Begin replied in the same session. The visit opened direct Egyptian-Israeli negotiations.

title: Peace Now founded
summary: Peace Now was founded in 1978, during the negotiations with Egypt, to press for a peace agreement. It became a leading Israeli movement advocating territorial compromise and a two-state solution.

title: Coastal Road massacre
summary: Fatah gunmen who landed by boat hijacked a bus on the coastal highway on 11 March 1978; 38 Israeli civilians, including 13 children, were killed and more than 70 wounded. Nine attackers were killed and two captured.

title: Operation Litani
summary: Three days after the Coastal Road attack Israel invaded southern Lebanon up to the Litani River against PLO bases. Norton estimates about 1,100 people were killed, most of them Palestinian and Lebanese civilians. On 19 March the Security Council (resolution 425) called on Israel to withdraw and created UNIFIL.

title: Israel wins Eurovision 1978
summary: 'A-Ba-Ni-Bi' by Izhar Cohen and the Alphabeta won the Eurovision Song Contest in Paris on 22 April 1978 with 157 points, Israel's first win.

title: Ariel founded
summary: Ariel was established in 1978 in the central West Bank south of Nablus.

title: Camp David Accords
summary: After 13 days of talks hosted by US President Carter, Begin and Sadat signed two frameworks on 17 September 1978: one for an Egypt-Israel peace treaty based on full Israeli withdrawal from Sinai, and one for Palestinian autonomy in the West Bank and Gaza, which was never implemented. Begin agreed to let the Knesset decide on evacuating the Sinai settlements.

choices.label: Accept full withdrawal from Sinai, including settlements, in exchange for full peace
choices.note: The framework provided for full withdrawal; Begin put the settlements to the Knesset (S218, S244).

choices.label: Insist on keeping the Rafah-salient settlements such as Yamit
choices.note: Begin's opening position before Camp David (S244).

title: Nobel Peace Prize to Begin and Sadat
summary: The 1978 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded jointly to Menachem Begin and Anwar Sadat for the Camp David agreements.

title: Iran severs relations after the revolution
title_he: איראן מנתקת את היחסים עם ישראל
summary: After the Islamic Revolution of February 1979 Iran cut its ties with Israel and handed the Israeli mission in Tehran to the PLO; Israeli-Iranian contacts nonetheless continued covertly, including arms sales during the Iran-Iraq war.

title: Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty
summary: Begin and Sadat signed the peace treaty in Washington on 26 March 1979, witnessed by President Carter. Israel would withdraw from all of Sinai within three years, normal relations and an exchange of ambassadors would follow the interim withdrawal, and Israeli shipping gained free passage through the Suez Canal and the Strait of Tiran. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League from 1979 to 1989.

title: Israel wins Eurovision 1979 in Jerusalem
summary: Hosting the contest in Jerusalem on 31 March 1979, Israel won again with 'Hallelujah' by Milk and Honey with Gali Atari, scoring 125 points.

title: Israel and Egypt exchange ambassadors
summary: Following the interim withdrawal in Sinai, Israel and Egypt established full diplomatic relations and exchanged ambassadors in February 1980; regular flights began the next month.

title: Shekel replaces the Israeli pound
summary: Amid triple-digit inflation, the shekel replaced the Israeli pound (lira) on 24 February 1980 at a rate of ten pounds to one shekel.

title: Car bombs maim West Bank mayors
summary: On 2 June 1980 car bombs planted by members of a Jewish settler underground maimed the mayors of Nablus, Bassam Shakaa, who lost both legs, and Ramallah, Karim Khalaf. The perpetrators were identified only in 1984.

title: Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel
summary: The Knesset passed a Basic Law on 30 July 1980 declaring 'Jerusalem, complete and united' the capital of Israel. The Security Council in resolution 478 (20 August 1980) censured the law, declared it null and void and called on states with embassies in Jerusalem to withdraw them.

title: Operation Opera: strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor
summary: Eight Israeli F-16s escorted by F-15s destroyed the nearly completed Osirak (Tammuz) research reactor near Baghdad on 7 June 1981; ten Iraqi soldiers and a French technician were killed. The Security Council unanimously condemned the attack in resolution 487 and the United States briefly suspended F-16 deliveries.

choices.label: Destroy the reactor by air strike before it is fuelled
choices.note: Cabinet approved in October 1980 by 10-6; Sharon among advocates (S251).

choices.label: Rely on covert sabotage and diplomacy with France
choices.note: Favoured by intelligence chief Saguy; Dayan, Weizman and Yadin opposed a strike (S251).

title: Election to the Tenth Knesset
summary: Likud won 48 seats to the Alignment's 47 on 30 June 1981. Begin formed a narrow 61-member coalition with the National Religious Party, Tami and Agudat Yisrael, sworn in on 5 August 1981.

title: Sadat assassinated
summary: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat was killed by members of Egyptian Islamic Jihad during a military parade on 6 October 1981. His successor Hosni Mubarak maintained the peace treaty.

title: Golan Heights Law
summary: On 14 December 1981 the Knesset voted 63-21 to apply Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the Golan Heights. The Security Council unanimously declared the decision 'null and void and without international legal effect' (resolution 497); the United States suspended a newly signed strategic-cooperation memorandum. Most of the Golan's roughly 14,000 Druze residents struck in protest, and a longer strike followed in 1982.

choices.label: Apply Israeli law to the Golan
Keep military administration pending negotiations with Syria
choices.note: The status quo since 1967, preferred by the bill's opponents (S252, S253).

title: Yamit evacuated; Sinai returned to Egypt
summary: Under the peace treaty Israel evacuated its Sinai settlements; the official evacuation of Yamit began on 23 April 1982 against resistance by some residents and protesters, and the army demolished most of the buildings. The withdrawal from Sinai was completed on 25 April 1982.

choices.label: Evacuate the settlements on schedule as the treaty requires
choices.note: Evacuation began 23 April 1982 (S254).

choices.label: Delay the final withdrawal and seek to renegotiate the Rafah salient
choices.note: Demanded by opponents of the withdrawal (S254).

title: 1982 Lebanon War (Operation Peace for Galilee)
summary: After the attempted assassination of Ambassador Shlomo Argov in London by the Abu Nidal group, Israel invaded Lebanon on 6 June 1982 with a declared aim of pushing the PLO 40 km north; forces fought Syria and besieged West Beirut until more than 14,000 PLO fighters were evacuated in August-September. Lebanese tallies of the dead for June-August 1982 range from 17,285 (An-Nahar) to 19,085 (Lebanese authorities), many of them civilians; Gabriel estimated 5,000-8,000 civilian deaths. Israel lost 368 soldiers by October 1982 and 654 by June 1985.

choices.label: Launch a broad invasion that extends to Beirut
choices.note: The war expanded beyond the declared 40 km aim (S255).

choices.label: Limit the operation to a 40-km zone north of the border
choices.note: The aim the cabinet approved on 5 June 1982 (S255).

choices.label: Respond to the Argov shooting with air strikes only
choices.note: Israel bombed PLO targets on 4-5 June before the invasion (S255).

title: Lebanese President-elect Bashir Gemayel assassinated
summary: Bashir Gemayel, the Phalange leader elected president of Lebanon on 23 August 1982 with Israeli backing, was killed with about 26 others by a bomb at Phalange headquarters in Beirut on 14 September 1982. A member of the Syrian Social Nationalist Party was later identified as the bomber. The IDF entered West Beirut the next day.

title: Sabra and Shatila massacre
summary: Between 16 and 18 September 1982 Lebanese Phalangist militiamen, admitted by the IDF into the Sabra neighbourhood and Shatila refugee camp in Israeli-controlled West Beirut, killed Palestinian and Lebanese Shia civilians. Death-toll estimates range from 460 (Lebanese army prosecutor) and 700-800 (Israeli intelligence) to more than 2,000 (Palestinian Red Crescent) and 3,000-3,500 (Kapeliouk; al-Hout). The killings caused a political crisis in Israel.

title: Mass protest in Tel Aviv demands inquiry
summary: On 25 September 1982 a rally organised by Peace Now in Tel Aviv demanded a state commission of inquiry into Sabra and Shatila and the resignation of Defence Minister Sharon; organisers put the crowd at about 400,000. The government appointed the Kahan Commission days later.

title: IDF headquarters in Tyre destroyed
summary: An explosion destroyed the Israeli military headquarters in Tyre on 11 November 1982, killing 76 Israeli soldiers, Shin Bet agents and Border Police and 15 Lebanese detainees (2024 figures; earlier counts of detainees varied). Israel long attributed the blast to gas cylinders; a 2024 IDF inquiry found a car bomb 'highly probable'. A suicide truck bomb at the Shin Bet building in Tyre on 4 November 1983 killed 28 Israelis and 32 Lebanese prisoners.

title: Neve Dekalim founded in the Gaza Strip
summary: Neve Dekalim was founded in 1983 in the Gush Katif bloc of the southern Gaza Strip and became the largest Israeli settlement there until the 2005 disengagement.

title: Kahan Commission report
summary: The state commission of inquiry headed by Supreme Court President Yitzhak Kahan found Israel indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila killings and Defence Minister Ariel Sharon personally responsible for disregarding the danger of bloodshed; it recommended his removal. Sharon left the defence ministry but remained in the cabinet as minister without portfolio.

title: 17 May Agreement with Lebanon
summary: US-mediated talks produced an agreement on 17 May 1983 ending the state of war between Israel and Lebanon and providing for Israeli withdrawal. Under Syrian pressure Lebanon abrogated it in March 1984.

title: Bank shares crisis
summary: Israel's major banks had for years propped up their own share prices. When the shares began to collapse, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange closed for 18 days from 6 October 1983, and the government undertook to buy bank shares from the public, effectively nationalising the main banks. The Bejski Commission reported on the affair in April 1986.

choices.label: Guarantee the value of bank shares and take over the banks ('the arrangement')
choices.note: The state's share-purchase arrangement (S262).

choices.label: Let bank share prices fall without a state guarantee
choices.note: The alternative analysed by Blass and Grossman (S262).

title: Begin resigns; Yitzhak Shamir becomes Prime Minister
title_he: התפטרות בגין ויצחק שמיר לראשות הממשלה
summary: Menachem Begin, who had withdrawn from public life after his wife's death in November 1982 and amid the protracted Lebanon war, resigned in 1983. Yitzhak Shamir formed the Twentieth Government on 10 October 1983.

title: Bus 300 affair
summary: Four Palestinians hijacked an Egged bus on 12 April 1984; in the rescue the next morning two were killed and two captured alive, who were then killed on the orders of Shin Bet chief Avraham Shalom. A press photograph exposed the cover-up; Shalom and other officers received presidential pardons in 1986.

title: Jewish Underground uncovered
summary: The Shin Bet arrested members of a settler underground in late April 1984 after they planted bombs on Arab buses in East Jerusalem. The group was responsible for the 1980 car bombings of West Bank mayors and the July 1983 attack on the Islamic College in Hebron that killed three students, and had planned to blow up the Dome of the Rock.

title: 1984 election and the rotation government
summary: The Alignment won 44 seats and Likud 41 on 23 July 1984; neither bloc could form a government. A national unity government was formed on 13 September 1984 with Shimon Peres as prime minister for two years and Yitzhak Shamir for the next two, and Yitzhak Rabin as defence minister throughout.

choices.label: Form a national unity government with a rotating premiership
choices.note: Outcome of the 1984 deadlock (S214).

choices.label: Attempt a narrow Alignment-led coalition
choices.note: Neither bloc had a majority (S214).

choices.label: Attempt a narrow Likud-led coalition
choices.note: Neither bloc had a majority (S214).

title: Operation Moses
summary: Between 21 November 1984 and 5 January 1985 about 8,000 Ethiopian Jews who had trekked to refugee camps in Sudan were airlifted to Israel. Many died on the journey and in the camps. The airlift stopped after it became public; about 500 more were brought out in the US-led Operation Joshua in 1985.

title: US-Israel Free Trade Agreement
title_he: הסכם סחר חופשי עם ארצות הברית
summary: Israel and the United States signed the first US free-trade agreement on 22 April 1985; tariffs were phased out so that all eligible Israeli products entered the US duty-free from 1995.

title: Jibril prisoner exchange
summary: On 21 May 1985 the unity government released 1,150 prisoners, including Lod attacker Kozo Okamoto and Gaza cleric Ahmed Yassin, in exchange for three soldiers held by Ahmed Jibril's PFLP-General Command. The deal drew heavy public criticism.

choices.label: Release 1,150 prisoners to bring home the three soldiers
choices.note: Approved by all ministers except Yitzhak Navon (S266).

choices.label: Refuse a deal on these terms
choices.note: The position of the deal's critics (S266).

title: Withdrawal to the south Lebanon 'security zone'
summary: Following a January 1985 cabinet decision, the IDF withdrew in stages from most of Lebanon by June 1985, keeping a 'security zone' along the border held with the South Lebanon Army. Israel had lost 654 soldiers in Lebanon since June 1982.

choices.label: Withdraw to a security zone held with the South Lebanon Army
choices.note: Unity government decision of January 1985 (S244).

choices.label: Withdraw completely to the international border
choices.note: Option debated in 1985 and carried out only in 2000 (S244, S246).

title: Economic Stabilization Plan
summary: With inflation at about 445% in 1984 and rising, the unity government adopted an emergency stabilisation plan on 1 July 1985: a sharp devaluation followed by a fixed exchange rate, deep budget cuts, a wage agreement with the Histadrut, temporary price controls and limits on central-bank financing of the deficit. Inflation fell to around 20% within about two years.

choices.label: Adopt a comprehensive shock programme agreed with the Histadrut and employers
choices.note: The 1 July 1985 plan (S267).

choices.label: Peg the economy to the US dollar (dollarisation)
choices.note: Proposed by Finance Minister Aridor in 1983 and rejected (S267).

choices.label: Continue short-term wage-price 'package deals'
choices.note: The 1984-85 package deals had failed to stop inflation (S267).

title: New Israeli shekel introduced
summary: As part of stabilisation, new shekel notes and coins were issued from 4 September 1985 at 1,000 old shekels to one new shekel.

title: Operation Wooden Leg: raid on PLO headquarters in Tunis
summary: Days after three Israelis were killed on a yacht in Larnaca, Cyprus, Israeli aircraft bombed the PLO headquarters at Hammam Chott near Tunis on 1 October 1985. Reported deaths range from 47 to about 71, including PLO members and Tunisian civilians. The Security Council condemned the raid in resolution 573, with the United States abstaining.

title: Pollard espionage affair
summary: US Navy intelligence analyst Jonathan Pollard was arrested on 21 November 1985 outside the Israeli embassy in Washington for passing classified material to Israel. Israel apologised and initially described the operation as unauthorised; Pollard was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1987.

title: Vanunu reveals Dimona secrets
summary: Former Dimona technician Mordechai Vanunu gave The Sunday Times details and photographs of the Negev Nuclear Research Center, published on 5 October 1986. He had been lured to Rome and abducted by Mossad on 30 September; he was convicted in a closed trial in 1988 and sentenced to 18 years.

title: Rotation: Shamir becomes Prime Minister
summary: Under the 1984 coalition agreement Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Shamir exchanged posts; Shamir's Twenty-Second Government took office on 20 October 1986.

title: Lavi fighter's first flight
summary: The first prototype of the Lavi, an Israeli-designed multirole fighter developed by Israel Aircraft Industries from 1980 with US funding, flew on 31 December 1986. The cabinet cancelled the programme on 30 August 1987 by 12 votes to 11.

title: Lavi fighter programme cancelled
summary: Israel's national-unity cabinet voted on 30 August 1987, by 12 to 11 with one abstention, to stop development of the IAI Lavi, the Israeli-designed fighter then in flight testing. Cost was the main argument against continuing.

choices.label: Cancel the Lavi and buy more F-16s
choices.note: The majority view in the unity cabinet, carried 12–11 with one abstention.

choices.label: Continue building the Lavi
choices.note: Position of the programme's supporters in cabinet, led by Moshe Arens, who lost the vote.

title: First Intifada begins
summary: A Palestinian popular uprising against Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza Strip broke out in December 1987 after a traffic accident in Gaza involving an Israeli truck, and lasted until the Oslo Declaration of September 1993. B'Tselem counts 1,070 Palestinians (237 of them minors) killed by Israeli security forces and 54 by Israeli civilians between 9 December 1987 and 13 September 1993; other estimates run to about 1,200–1,280. Israeli deaths are given as about 160–180 (B'Tselem) to about 200 (official Israeli figures).

title: Hamas founded
summary: The Islamic Resistance Movement (Hamas) was founded in Gaza at the start of the first intifada, organised in part by members of the Muslim Brotherhood under Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. Hamas literature dates its founding to 8 December 1987; some historians place the founding meeting on 9 December.

title: Abu Jihad killed in Tunis
summary: Khalil al-Wazir (Abu Jihad), deputy to PLO chairman Yasser Arafat and a senior organiser of the intifada, was shot dead at his home in Tunis by Israeli commandos. Israel did not acknowledge the operation until a 2012 Israeli press report described it as Mossad-planned and carried out by Sayeret Matkal.

title: Jordan severs ties with the West Bank
summary: King Hussein announced that Jordan was severing its legal and administrative ties with the West Bank after 38 years of union of the two banks, deferring to the PLO as representative of the Palestinians.

title: Ofek-1: Israel's first satellite
summary: Israel launched its first satellite, Ofek-1, aboard the Israeli-built Shavit launcher.

title: Election to the 12th Knesset
summary: Likud won 40 seats and the Alignment 39. Despite a 65-seat right-wing and religious bloc, coalition talks foundered on religious-legislation demands, and Yitzhak Shamir formed another national-unity government with Shimon Peres, this time without a rotation of the premiership.

title: Palestinian Declaration of Independence
summary: At its 19th session in Algiers, the Palestine National Council proclaimed a State of Palestine; the text, drafted by poet Mahmoud Darwish, was read by Yasser Arafat.

title: Mass immigration from the (former) Soviet Union
summary: After Soviet emigration restrictions were lifted, about 185,000 immigrants from the USSR arrived in 1990 alone and roughly 980,000 between 1989 and 2006 (Tolts). Israeli CBS counts 906,500 immigrants of all origins in 1990–2001, 86% of them from the former USSR.

title: Unity government falls; Shamir forms narrow coalition
title_he: נפילת ממשלת האחדות והקמת ממשלה צרה
summary: The Shamir–Peres national-unity government formed after the 1988 election collapsed in March 1990. In June 1990 Shamir formed a narrow government of right-wing and religious parties.

title: Iraqi Scud missiles strike Israel
summary: During the Gulf War, Iraq fired 39 Scud missiles at Israel in 19 attacks between 18 January and late February 1991, mainly at Tel Aviv and Haifa, aiming to draw Israel into the war and split the US-led coalition. Residents sheltered in sealed rooms with gas masks; direct deaths were in the single digits, and accounts that include indirect deaths give higher totals. At US request Israel did not retaliate, and the US deployed Patriot batteries in Israel.

choices.label: Hold fire at US request and accept Patriot batteries
choices.note: Shamir's decision, taken to avoid fracturing the coalition, which included Arab states.

choices.label: Launch a retaliatory air operation in western Iraq
choices.note: Defence Minister Moshe Arens pressed for a strike and approved an operation plan; Shamir delayed and it was not carried out.

title: Operation Solomon
summary: As rebel forces closed in on Addis Ababa, Israel airlifted some 14,300 Ethiopian Jews (JDC: just over 14,000; other accounts 14,325) to Israel in about 36 hours on 24–25 May 1991, using Israeli Air Force and El Al aircraft under military censorship.

title: Madrid Peace Conference
summary: The US and USSR convened a peace conference in Madrid (30 October – 4 November 1991) at which Israel sat for the first time at the same table with Syria, Lebanon, Egypt and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation. It launched bilateral and multilateral tracks; the bilateral Washington talks had stalled by 1993.

title: Basic Laws on human dignity and freedom of occupation
title_he: חוקי היסוד: כבוד האדם וחירותו וחופש העיסוק
summary: In its final weeks the 12th Knesset passed Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty (17 March 1992) and Basic Law: Freedom of Occupation, the first Basic Laws protecting individual rights. The same Knesset also enacted direct election of the prime minister, first used in 1996.

title: Labor wins; Rabin becomes prime minister
title_he: הבחירות לכנסת ה-13 – רבין ראש ממשלה
summary: Labor under Yitzhak Rabin won 44 seats to Likud's 32 in the election to the 13th Knesset, in which the threshold had been raised to 1.5%. Rabin formed a Labor-led government that went on to negotiate with the PLO and Jordan.

title: Deportation of 415 Palestinians to Marj al-Zuhur
title_he: גירוש 415 פעילי חמאס לג'בל מרג' א-זוהור
summary: After the kidnapping and killing of Border Police officer Nissim Toledano by Hamas, the Rabin government deported 415 Palestinians identified as Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists to south Lebanon; the High Court allowed the order 5–2. Lebanon refused them entry and they camped at Marj al-Zuhur. Security Council resolution 799 condemned the deportation, and under a February 1993 arrangement with the US Israel agreed to an early return; several deportees, including Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, later led Hamas.

displacement.note: Deportees, returned in 1993; Palestinian sources say 418 were ordered

title: Operation Accountability in Lebanon
summary: After Hezbollah attacks on Israeli forces and rocket fire on northern Israel, the IDF carried out a week-long air and artillery campaign in south Lebanon, warning civilians in the south to leave. Lebanese official sources counted 118 civilians killed; the US State Department reported over 150 killed and some 300,000 people displaced for about a week. A US-brokered understanding ended it on 31 July.

displacement.note: US State Dept: over 300,000 displaced for about one week

title: Oslo Accords: Declaration of Principles
summary: After secret talks in Norway, Israel and the PLO, which had exchanged letters of recognition, signed the Declaration of Principles on the White House lawn. It provided for an elected Palestinian interim self-government in the West Bank and Gaza for a transitional period of up to five years, with permanent-status issues (Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, borders) left to later negotiation.

choices.label: Recognise the PLO and sign the Declaration of Principles
choices.note: Rabin and Peres approved the Oslo back channel and signed with the PLO.

choices.label: Keep to the Madrid-format Washington talks without the PLO
choices.note: The existing official track negotiated with a Jordanian-Palestinian delegation; it had stalled by 1993.

title: Cave of the Patriarchs massacre
summary: On Purim, Baruch Goldstein, a physician from Kiryat Arba and Kach activist, opened fire on Muslim worshippers at prayer in the Ibrahimi Mosque/Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron, killing 29 and wounding about 125–129 before he was overpowered and killed. The government appointed the Shamgar Commission, which found that he acted alone and criticised security arrangements at the site.

title: Gaza–Jericho Agreement (Cairo)
summary: Rabin and Arafat signed in Cairo the agreement implementing the first stage of Oslo: Israeli forces withdrew from most of the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area within weeks, and authority there passed to the new Palestinian Authority, with an annexed protocol on economic relations (Paris Protocol). Israeli settlements and military locations in Gaza remained under Israeli control.

title: Nobel Peace Prize to Rabin, Peres and Arafat
title_he: פרס נובל לשלום לרבין, פרס וערפאת
summary: The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 1994 Peace Prize jointly to Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat for their efforts to create peace in the Middle East; the prize was presented in Oslo on 10 December 1994.

title: Dizengoff Street bus bombing
summary: A Hamas suicide bomber blew up a No. 5 Dan bus on Dizengoff Street in Tel Aviv, killing 22 people (21 Israelis and a Dutch national) and injuring dozens; at the time it was the deadliest suicide bombing in Israel.

title: Peace treaty with Jordan
summary: Prime ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Abdelsalam al-Majali signed the Israel–Jordan Treaty of Peace at the Arava/Araba crossing north of Eilat, witnessed by the United States and Russia, ending the state of war, fixing the international border and setting water-sharing arrangements for the Jordan and Yarmuk rivers.

title: Oslo II Interim Agreement
summary: Israel and the PLO signed the Interim Agreement in Washington, dividing the West Bank into Area A (full Palestinian civil and security control, initially about 3% of the territory and including the main Palestinian towns), Area B (Palestinian civil, joint security control, about 24%) and Area C (Israeli control, about 73%), and providing for Palestinian elections. After later redeployments Area A reached about 18%.

title: Assassination of Yitzhak Rabin
summary: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead by Yigal Amir, a Jewish Israeli opponent of the Oslo process, as he left a peace rally at Kings of Israel Square in Tel Aviv. Shimon Peres succeeded him. Amir was sentenced to life imprisonment in March 1996; the Shamgar Commission found serious security lapses but no conspiracy.

title: Mizrahi Bank ruling – 'constitutional revolution'
summary: In United Mizrahi Bank v. Migdal Cooperative Village, a nine-justice Supreme Court panel led by Aharon Barak held that the 1992 Basic Laws have constitutional status and that courts may set aside ordinary legislation conflicting with them, establishing judicial review of Knesset laws. Supporters and critics alike call it the 'constitutional revolution'.

title: Wave of suicide bombings in Jerusalem, Ashkelon and Tel Aviv
summary: In nine days Hamas suicide bombings killed about 60 people: 26 on Jerusalem bus 18 and one at an Ashkelon junction on 25 February, 19 on another bus 18 on 3 March, and 13–14 at Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Center on 4 March (UN tally 61). Hamas presented them as revenge for Israel's January killing of bomb-maker Yahya Ayyash. Leaders of 29 countries met at a 'Summit of the Peacemakers' in Sharm el-Sheikh on 13 March.

title: Operation Grapes of Wrath and the Qana shelling
title_he: מבצע ענבי זעם והפגזת כפר קנא
summary: Following Hezbollah rocket fire on northern Israel, the IDF launched a 16-day air and artillery campaign in Lebanon, again seeking to displace civilians from the south. On 18 April Israeli shells struck the UNIFIL Fijian battalion compound at Qana, where about 800 civilians sheltered, killing more than 100 (commonly given as 106). A UN military adviser found it unlikely that the shelling resulted from technical or procedural error; the IDF attributed it to operational mistakes. A cease-fire understanding was announced on 26 April.

title: First direct election of the prime minister: Netanyahu
title_he: הבחירה הישירה הראשונה לראשות הממשלה – נתניהו
summary: In the first election held under the direct-election system, Benjamin Netanyahu defeated Shimon Peres by about 30,000 votes (50.5% to 49.5%). In the Knesset vote Labor won 34 seats and the Likud–Gesher–Tzomet list 32.

title: Western Wall tunnel clashes
summary: The government's opening of a new northern exit to the Western Wall tunnel in Jerusalem's Old City set off Palestinian protests and armed clashes across the West Bank and Gaza. By early October 15 Israelis and at least 57 Palestinians had been killed.

title: Hebron Protocol
summary: Netanyahu and Arafat concluded the Protocol Concerning the Redeployment in Hebron: about 80% of the city (H-1) passed to Palestinian control, while H-2, including the Jewish settler enclaves and the Cave of the Patriarchs, remained under Israeli control; a large Palestinian population lives in both areas.

title: Helicopter disaster at She'ar Yashuv
summary: Two Israeli Air Force CH-53 'Yas'ur' transport helicopters carrying troops to the south Lebanon security zone collided over She'ar Yashuv in the Upper Galilee, killing all 73 soldiers and aircrew aboard.

title: Failed attempt on Khaled Mashal in Amman
summary: Mossad agents tried to kill Hamas political leader Khaled Mashal in Amman by spraying a poison into his ear; two agents were caught. Under pressure from King Hussein and President Clinton, Israel supplied the antidote and freed Hamas founder Sheikh Ahmed Yassin in exchange for the agents, a crisis in relations with Jordan three years after the peace treaty.

choices.label: Supply the antidote and release Sheikh Yassin to recover the agents
choices.note: Netanyahu's decision after King Hussein's demand and US intervention.

choices.label: Refuse Jordan's demands
choices.note: The alternative Jordan threatened against: King Hussein made the antidote a condition of keeping the peace relationship intact.

title: Dana International wins Eurovision
summary: Dana International won the Eurovision Song Contest in Birmingham for Israel with 'Diva', scoring 172 points in the first contest decided entirely by televote; she was the contest's first transgender winner.

title: AOL buys Mirabilis (ICQ)
summary: America Online agreed to buy Mirabilis, the start-up founded in 1996 by five young Israelis that created the ICQ instant-messaging program, for $287 million plus up to $120 million in performance payments, a landmark exit in Israel's emerging technology sector.

title: Wye River Memorandum
summary: At a US-hosted summit at Wye River, Maryland, Netanyahu and Arafat agreed on further Israeli redeployment in the West Bank—13% of territory to move out of Area C and 14.2% from Area B to Area A—linked to Palestinian security commitments.

title: Barak elected prime minister
summary: Ehud Barak of One Israel defeated Netanyahu by a wide margin in the direct prime-ministerial vote. The Knesset was fragmented: One Israel 26 seats, Likud 19, Shas 17.

title: Withdrawal from south Lebanon
summary: The IDF withdrew from the south Lebanon security zone, completing the pullout on 24 May 2000, ahead of the July deadline set by Barak's cabinet. The Israeli-allied South Lebanon Army collapsed; some members and their families fled to Israel and others surrendered to Hezbollah, which took over the area.

choices.label: Withdraw unilaterally to the international border
choices.note: Barak's cabinet decision, which had set a July 2000 deadline for withdrawal.

choices.label: Stay in the security zone until an agreement with Syria
choices.note: The earlier policy: the zone was held pending a Syria–Lebanon settlement; casualty figures here are illustrative game values, not historical.

title: Camp David summit
summary: President Clinton hosted Barak and Arafat at Camp David for final-status talks. The summit ended on 25 July without agreement, with Jerusalem and the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif and Palestinian refugees the central disputes.
